title: Searching for a Target in a Rotated Sorted Array

phrases.explanation: The sorted array has been shifted so that elements wrap around from the end to the beginning
Reduce the range of elements we need to examine to find the answer
Determining whether the left portion or right portion of the array maintains ascending order
The target value lies between the minimum and maximum of a sorted segment
A special or unusual input scenario that might cause incorrect behavior

technical_terms.definition: A sorted array that has been split at a pivot index and the two halves swapped in order
An algorithm that repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target to the middle element
The index where the rotation occurred, separating two sorted subsequences

concept: Given an integer array that was sorted in ascending order and then rotated at an unknown pivot, find the index of a given target value. Return negative one if the target is not present. All elements are unique.

solutions.label: Linear Scan
solutions.summary: Scan every element in the array and check if it matches the target.

solutions.label: Find Pivot then Binary Search
solutions.summary: First locate the pivot point using binary search, then run standard binary search on the correct half.

solutions.label: Single-Pass Modified Binary Search
solutions.summary: Use one binary search that determines which half is sorted at each step and decides which half to search next.

sections.diagram:

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Imagine you have a sorted array of unique integers, but it has been rotated at some unknown pivot. For example, the array one, two, four, five, six, seven, zero becomes four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two. Given such an array and a target value, return the index of the target, or negative one if it is not found.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So all elements are unique, and the array was originally sorted in ascending order before being rotated. Can the array be empty, and what should I return in that case?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the array could be empty, and you should return negative one. The array contains only unique integers and can have up to ten thousand elements.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What if the array was not rotated at all, meaning it is still fully sorted? Should my solution handle that too?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, treat a non-rotated array as a valid input. It is essentially rotated by zero positions.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I need to search for a target in a rotated sorted array of unique integers and return its index, or negative one if absent. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

sections.title: Linear Scan
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    A["4"] --> B["5"] --> C["6"] --> D["7"] --> E["0 ✓"]
    E --> F["1"] --> G["2"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#22c55e,color:#fff
    style F fill:#9ca3af,color:#fff
    style G fill:#9ca3af,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is a linear scan. I iterate through every element and check if it equals the target. For the array four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two with target zero, I check each element until I find zero at index four.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. What is the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n since we may need to visit every element. The space complexity is O of one because we only use a loop variable.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: This ignores the fact that the array is mostly sorted. Can you do better?

sections.title: Find Pivot then Binary Search
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2"] --> B{"Find pivot with binary search"}
    B --> C["Pivot at index 4: value 0"]
    C --> D{"Target 0 <= 2? Right half"}
    D --> E["Binary search indices 4 to 6"]
    E --> F["Found 0 at index 4"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style F fill:#22c55e,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since the array has two sorted halves, I can first find the pivot point using binary search. The pivot is where the smallest element is. I compare the middle element to the rightmost element. If the middle is greater, the pivot is to the right. Otherwise it is to the left.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For our example, four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two, I find the pivot at index four where the value is zero. Now I know the left sorted half is indices zero to three and the right sorted half is indices four to six.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I check whether the target falls within the right half by comparing it to the last element. Since zero is less than or equal to two, I binary search the right half and find zero at index four.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. This runs two binary searches, so the time complexity is O of log n. Can you do it in a single pass?

sections.title: Single-Pass Modified Binary Search
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: 4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2 — target 0"] --> B["left=0, right=6, mid=3, value=7"]
    B --> C{"Left half 4..7 is sorted"}
    C -->|"0 not in 4..7"| D["Move left to mid+1=4"]
    D --> E["left=4, right=6, mid=5, value=1"]
    E --> F{"Left half 0..1 is sorted"}
    F -->|"0 in range 0..1"| G["Move right to mid-1=4"]
    G --> H["left=4, right=4, mid=4, value=0 ✓"]
    style A fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style B fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style E fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H fill:#22c55e,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can solve this with a single modified binary search. At each step, I check which half of the array is sorted by comparing the left boundary to the middle. Then I check if the target falls within that sorted half.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Using our array, four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two, with target zero. Left is zero, right is six, mid is three with value seven. The left half from four to seven is sorted. Zero is not between four and seven, so I move left to mid plus one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Now left is four, right is six, mid is five with value one. The left half from zero to one is sorted. Zero falls within zero to one, so I move right to mid minus one. Now left equals right equals four, and the value is zero. Found it!

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. This runs in O of log n time with O of one space, and you only need a single binary search loop. Very clean.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    A["Linear Scan
O of n time
O of 1 space"] --> B["Find Pivot + Binary Search
O of log n time
O of 1 space"]
    B --> C["Single-Pass Binary Search
O of log n time
O of 1 space"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. You started with a linear scan at O of n, improved to a two-pass binary search at O of log n, and then combined everything into a single elegant binary search pass.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that even in a rotated array, at least one half around the midpoint is always sorted. By identifying the sorted half, we can decide which direction to search, keeping the O of log n guarantee.
